skip_reason: Existing-move logistics only — not a sales call. Inbound date-change request on an already-booked job. The customer opened with 'I got a quote for moving on October something October 1st or second I think cause we were going to close then but our closing got moved up and so I'm hopeful you can tell me if you guys can accommodate the new date,' and the entire five minutes is Dustin locating the existing profile (which turned out to be under her husband's email, Will Taylor), checking the twenty-third and twenty-fourth, moving the booking, confirming the arrival window, and promising an updated confirmation email. There is no quote being built, no rate or hourly pricing discussed, no clock explanation, no inventory or access probe, no estimate presented, no differentiator pitch, and no booking attempt, because the job was already on the schedule and the customer was already sold — she said 'I will go ahead and sign a contract like now' in the second sentence. The work is real and it retained a two-day pack-and-move job, but the 85-point sales scorecard has nothing to measure here; scoring it literally would produce a meaningless number and pull the run average down for a call the rep handled correctly.
top_strength: Dustin turned a five-minute administrative task into a relationship moment, which is exactly what a date change should be. The customer arrived slightly apologetic and venting about her husband — 'my husband originally called but god bless him. He can't be trusted to keep going with it... I was like, did you call the movers? Did you call the movers? And he's like, no, oh, I got to do that' — and Dustin met it instantly with 'My wife would definitely say the same thing about me,' which got her laughing and set the tone for everything after. He also removed the customer's own stated friction before she had to work for it. She said 'I will go ahead and sign a contract like now,' clearly braced for paperwork, and he took it straight off the table: 'We don't have a con, a contract you need to sign. That's no problem.' That is the no-friction differentiator landing naturally in the moment it mattered, without a script. He narrated the search honestly instead of going silent — 'Bear with me. I'm sorry for tracking you' — which mattered, because the profile was buried under her husband's email and she volunteered it ('It might be under my husband's email, which is W. Taylor 7686') precisely because he had kept her in the loop. When the booking tool fought him he said so plainly rather than pretending ('It's not letting me select the date. What is going on here? There we go, just need a little refresh') and, critically, he caught his own error before it shipped: 'Twenty fourth when I refreshed it. Went back to the old day... I almost didn't catch [that]. [You'd] have been calling back like dude, come on man.' Catching a silently-reverted date before sending the confirmation is the whole ballgame on a reschedule, and he caught it. He then confirmed both the two trucks on the twenty-third and the two on the twenty-fourth, sorted the email routing without making her re-explain the CC situation, and proactively answered the arrival-time question with the detail that actually helps: 'They should be getting over there between 8:30 and 9:00 in the morning. They'll give you a call when they're leaving the office, it should be about a thirty minute heads-up for you.' She ended the call twice saying 'Thank you so much I really appreciate it.'
coaching_note: Not scored — this is a reschedule on a booked job and it belongs outside the sales average. Dustin handled it well and there is no performance concern here; two small notes for the ops side rather than the sales side. First, the one genuine miss: the customer volunteered a change in scope and it was waved through. 'There's a lot of stuff we're not taking so I might need, I might need to have my mom here so what I'll do is I'll plan to label a bunch of [stuff]' drew only 'Okay, absolutely. That works.' On a packing job, 'a lot of stuff we're not taking' is a material change to the inventory the estimate was built on — it could move the pack day meaningfully in either direction, and it is exactly the kind of detail that surfaces as a surprise on move day. The right reply is thirty seconds long: 'That's a great plan, and it actually helps us a lot — if you can get anything that's staying into one room or tagged before we show up on the twenty-third, the crew will never have to stop and ask. Roughly how much of the house are we talking about? I want to make sure the estimate still reflects what we're actually packing.' That is a genuine Save-Your-Ass moment on a call that otherwise has no room for one, and it protects the estimate at the same time. Second, he committed to the updated confirmation email but never asked her to verify it — and this record needed verifying more than most. The profile was under her husband's name, she was CC'd on it only recently, he was momentarily unsure whether the email addresses matched ('Sweet and it looks like that might be a different email address. No that looks like the same one'), and he had just personally caught the system reverting a date on him. One line closes all of that: 'It'll hit both your inboxes in a few minutes — give the dates and the addresses at the top a quick look and reply if anything's off.' Worth reinforcing generally: on any call where the booking tool misbehaved, the confirmation email is the only proof the fix took, so the customer needs to be asked to read it. For Amanda: the tool behaviour itself is worth a note to Matisen. Dustin refreshed to make the date selectable and then the twenty-fourth silently reverted to the old date afterward. He caught it by re-reading. A different rep on a busier day does not, and the customer finds out when no crew shows up.
phone_presence_notes: Easy, genuinely funny and human throughout — he matched her joke about her husband with one about his own wife ('My wife would definitely say the same thing about me'), narrated the awkward search instead of going silent, laughed at his own near-miss on the date, and closed with 'We appreciate you,' leaving a customer who thanked him unprompted twice in the last ninety seconds.
